name: Karl Dönitz
role: German grand admiral, commander of the U-boat arm and Navy (1943-1945) and last head of state of Nazi Germany (1945)
summary: Dönitz was a career naval officer who called himself an adherent of the national and social ideas of National Socialism, swore loyalty to Hitler and led the Navy and briefly the state until capitulation. He opposed communism, praised the end of class struggle and German unification, and held that a soldier must obey. After 1945 he said the Fuehrer principle had proved wrong and that democratic government with legal guarantees suits a developed nation, while still defending his conduct and the German war effort.

property-fundamental.rationale: He testified that he and his finance minister agreed that the basis of future life is the absolute legal security of the individual and of private property.

strong-leader.rationale: At Nuremberg (1946) he called the Fuehrer principle wrong as a political principle after having thought it right in 1932, and his memoir (1958) calls it fatal without checks on power; he held the earlier view during the regime and the later one for over three decades.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: His memoir says national regeneration must rest on patriotism rooted in love of country, language, culture and history, and objects to re-education that distorts that history.

democracy-best.rationale: His memoir concludes that the democratic form of government, with its guarantees of individual liberty and legal security for all, is the right form for any highly developed nation; the text does not address voters choosing badly.

political-violence-never.rationale: His memoir says he cannot deny the moral right of Germans who committed high treason to save the country from Hitler and can sympathise with political murder when the doer risks his own life; he also treated the 1934 Roehm purge as a political necessity.

ethnic-nation.rationale: His memoir says the idea of a national community in the ethnological sense, uniting the German race, filled him with enthusiasm, and in 1946 he explained a 1944 remark as meaning the people's endurance was better preserved without Jewish elements.

single-common-good.rationale: He testified to the subordination of everyone to the interests of the common weal, and his memoir says he disliked Reichstag party interests being put ahead of the interest of the state.

class-collaboration.rationale: Testifying at Nuremberg he named the social side of National Socialism as no class struggle, with respect for every person whatever their class and each subordinated to the common weal; his memoir praises the end of class war under Hitler.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: His memoir's closing pages call for the regeneration, reunification and resurgence of the German people (written in the divided postwar Germany).

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: His memoir welcomes the incorporation of Austria and the Sudetenland as the fulfilment of a long German aim, which is approval of a claim to land beyond the borders inhabited by Germans.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: His memoir welcomes the union with Austria and the Sudetenland as a united Greater Germany, the dream of the forefathers, and calls the unification of the German peoples a fact deserving gratitude.

defeat-communism.rationale: His 1 May 1945 proclamation and order of the day made saving Germans from the Bolshevik enemy the aim of continuing the fight, and his memoir rejects communism as intolerable for the German people and praises Hitler's aim of keeping it out of Europe.

holocaust-denial.rationale: He testified that he first learned of the mass extermination from the indictment, and his memoir accepts the mass murders of the Hitler regime, saying he learned the full facts to his dismay after the war.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: He testified that a soldier obeys his oath and that refusing or plotting would be disobedience and treason, and his memoir calls it a moral duty of every fighter to back his government when it goes to war.

notes: Answers rest on his Nuremberg testimony and final statement (a defence, partly self-serving) and his memoir in Spanish translation. Words from 1944 (Heroes' Day speech) are known only through cross-examination. The Nuremberg judgment (juddoeni) was read but no statement is settled by it: it convicted him on waging aggressive war and breaches of naval law, which does not state a position on any test statement. Themes searched: economy, government, society, world, liberty, means; most economic, religious, gender and technology statements have no recorded position. A search for later interviews found only a 1975 press interview and no usable transcript.
